Exclusive

/ik-SKLOO-siv/ — rhymes with abusive · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something exclusive is limited to a select few people, often because it is expensive, high-status, or closed to the general public.

The rooftop lounge is exclusive — members only, and the waitlist is two years long.

Worked Example

The invitation-only gala featured only fifty guests from the city's wealthiest families, and tickets cost $5,000 each.

The word exclusive captures both the high-status barrier—you have to be wealthy or well-connected—and the sense of being shut out. Plain words like 'private' or 'limited' don't convey that prestige and desirability.

How Exclusive Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

private

private: not open to the general public

selective

selective: carefully choosing only a few entrants

elite

elite: reserved for a small privileged group

Antonyms

open

open: available to anyone who wants in

inclusive

inclusive: welcoming everyone and leaving no one out

How Strong Is It? — open → private → selective → exclusive

open vs. exclusive

open vs. exclusive: Open is the very opposite end of the scale from exclusive: an open event welcomes everyone, while an exclusive one admits only a chosen few.

private vs. exclusive

private vs. exclusive: Private is weaker than exclusive — a private gathering is simply not public, but an exclusive one deliberately shuts out all but a select, often privileged, few.

selective vs. exclusive

selective vs. exclusive: Selective is strong, but exclusive is stronger: a selective club chooses carefully among applicants, while an exclusive one keeps nearly everyone out by design.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-

Prefix — ex-: out (Latin)

Root — clus

Root — clus: to shut, close (Latin claudere) (Latin)

Suffix — -ive

Suffix — -ive: tending to; having the quality of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Ex- ('out') + clus ('shut') means 'shutting out'; with -ive ('tending to'), exclusive describes something that tends to shut people out, keeping entry limited to a select few.

Use the root in a new word: include

Use the root in a new word: include: Include comes from the same Latin root claudere, 'to shut': to include someone is to shut them in with the group, while an exclusive club shuts almost everyone out.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / neutral

Exclusive suggests both restriction AND prestige—use it when describing something limited to an elite few. For a simple restriction without the status element, choose 'private' or 'limited' instead.
